claims.text: The starting materials are multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles.
Rapid physical or chemical synthesis inherently produces slight nanoscale compositional and structural inhomogeneities in these nanoparticles.
Modified rapid quenching or pretreatment can increase initial compositional inhomogeneity relative to post-synthesis homogenization.
Localized nanoscale compositional fluctuations bias elemental diffusion.
Localized compositional fluctuations promote formation of a surface layer enriched in relatively noble or otherwise stabilizing elements.
Elevated temperature produces differential elemental diffusion from compositionally inhomogeneous regions.
Regions with locally elevated noble-metal content preferentially supply noble elements to the nanoparticle surface even when the overall noble-metal content is low.
The segregated surface layer passivates the nanoparticles.
The passivating surface layer retards nanoparticle coarsening and deleterious phase changes.
Nanoparticles with enhanced initial inhomogeneity will show faster and more pronounced surface aggregation of noble or stabilizing elements than homogenized nanoparticles.
Enhanced initial inhomogeneity will reduce the rates of coarsening and phase separation relative to the homogenized control.
Standard rapid synthesis yields moderate inhomogeneity, less distinct surface segregation, and greater high-temperature structural evolution than the enhanced-inhomogeneity treatment.
Alloy composition and annealing temperature can alter phase stability and the length scale of decomposition in multi-element alloys.
The proposed segregation-passivation effect is expected across near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticle systems at 773–1923 K.
Deviations from near-equiatomic composition or extreme processing conditions may modify or mask the proposed segregation-passivation behavior.
Highly oxidizing environments and reactive-gas partial pressures may modify or mask the proposed segregation-passivation behavior.
